name: Kızkalesi (Maiden's Castle)
desc: A Byzantine sea fort rebuilt by the Armenian kings of Cilicia, sitting on its own islet about 200 metres off a shallow sandy bay. You can swim, pedalo or take a boat out and walk the shell of towers with the water visible through the gateways. The town behind it is plain concrete holiday blocks.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the beach is wall-to-wall Adana and Konya families in August
tip: Swim out before nine in the morning; after ten the channel fills with pedalos and the boatmen start charging for the same crossing.
todo: Swim the 200 m out to the island
Walk the tower circuit inside the walls
Sunset from the beach with the castle lit
rev: Almost everyone rates the swim-to-a-castle novelty highly, then complains that the island interior is rubble with no shade, the town is architecturally grim, and August turns the bay into a car park.
entry: Free beach; boat return around ₺300 (≈€7) per person
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport near Adana, then about 2 h west on the D400 through Mersin; Mersin–Silifke minibuses drop you on the highway.

name: Korykos (Corycus)
desc: The land half of the Kızkalesi pair: a big ruined shore castle facing its island twin across a submerged causeway, with the wreck of a Roman and Byzantine port town spread behind it. The real find is the necropolis on the hill inland, hundreds of rock-cut tombs with carved doors, ploughs and reliefs of the dead.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the tombs are shadeless and the stone bakes in midsummer
tip: Cross the highway and walk fifteen minutes uphill into the necropolis; ninety percent of visitors never leave the castle by the beach.
todo: Land castle gatehouse and harbour wall
Rock-cut tombs on the inland hill
Adamkayalar reliefs in the gorge nearby
rev: Visitors like that it is free, unfenced and empty compared with the beach opposite, but warn about loose masonry, litter in the corners, thorns in the necropolis and no signage in any language.
entry: Free — the land castle is unstaffed
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 2 h west on the D400; it is a five-minute walk from the Kızkalesi beach strip.

name: Heaven and Hell Sinkholes
desc: Two collapsed karst chasms in the limestone above the coast. You take 452 steps down into Heaven to a fifth-century chapel of the Virgin built across the mouth of a cave, where an underground river roars out of the dark. Hell is a sheer unclimbable shaft you can only stare into from a steel platform.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the climb back out of Heaven in August is punishing
tip: Do the descent first thing in the morning and wear grippy shoes; the last stretch of steps to the cave mouth is wet, polished limestone.
todo: 452 steps down to the Virgin Mary chapel
Listen for the underground river at the cave mouth
Boardwalk into the Asthma Cave
rev: People find the scale genuinely startling and the chapel worth the knees, but complain about the return climb, the slippery final steps, the souvenir stalls at the top and queueing on summer weekends.
entry: ₺200 (≈€4.50) for the site, Asthma Cave a small extra fee
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 2 h west on the D400 and a 2 km climb up from Narlıkuyu; taxis wait at the junction.

name: Kanlıdivane
desc: An ancient town built around the rim of a limestone chasm 60 metres deep and the size of a football pitch. Five ruined basilicas stand at the edge, a Hellenistic tower carries a Greek dedication, and reliefs of a family and an armed soldier are cut into the sheer wall of the pit itself.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — no shade at all, and the plateau wind is welcome
tip: Walk the full rim anticlockwise to find the wall reliefs from above; from the main path they are invisible.
todo: Look down into the 60 m chasm
Find the reliefs cut in the pit wall
The four basilicas on the rim
rev: Those who make the detour call it the most atmospheric site on this coast and are surprised to have it to themselves; the gripes are the unmarked turning, the absent guardian and the total lack of railings.
entry: Small fee — check locally; often unstaffed
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 1 h 45 west on the D400 and 3 km inland at the Kumkuyu turning — you need a car.

name: Uzuncaburç (Diocaesarea)
desc: A temple city on a 1,200 m plateau where the ruins and the village share the same lanes. The Temple of Zeus Olbios carries some of the earliest Corinthian columns anywhere, thirty of them still standing, and a five-storey Hellenistic watchtower gives the village its name, meaning tall tower.
season: May–Oct — the plateau road can ice over in winter and the site empties
tip: Buy grape pekmez and tarhana from the village women at the temple gate; they are the reason the site is still lived in rather than fenced.
todo: Standing colonnade of the Temple of Zeus
Climb to the Hellenistic five-storey tower
The theatre and monumental gate
rev: Visitors rate it well above its visitor numbers and love the cool mountain air after the coast, while noting the 28 km of switchbacks from Silifke, the goats in the theatre and the thin explanatory signage.
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 2 h 30 to Silifke and a slow 45-min climb up the mountain road; a few daily minibuses run from Silifke.

name: Silifke
desc: A working river town under a Byzantine castle, built on Hellenistic Seleucia on the Calycadnus. A Roman bridge still crosses the Göksu, the columns of a temple of Jupiter stand in a side street, and a plaque by the water marks where Frederick Barbarossa drowned on crusade in 1190.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the valley is humid and heavy in high summer
tip: Drive up to the castle café for the evening view over the Göksu delta, then eat the local strained yoghurt with the town's own black carrot pickles.
todo: Castle terrace over the Göksu
Silifke Museum and its Meydancıkkale hoard
Birds in the Göksu Delta at dusk
rev: Travellers treat it as a base for Uzuncaburç and the delta and find the castle view better than expected, but say the town centre is traffic-heavy, plain, and short on decent places to sleep.
entry: Castle free; museum ₺150 (≈€3.50) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 2 h 30 west on the D400; frequent Mersin–Silifke buses take about 1 h 30 from Mersin otogar.

name: Narlıkuyu
desc: A cove the size of a courtyard where a karst spring surfaces straight into the sea and fish restaurants stand on stilts over the water. In a one-room building beside them lies the floor of a fourth-century bath house, a mosaic of the Three Graces that survived because a village well sat on top of it.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — lunchtimes in August need booking
tip: The mosaic building often shuts by five and over lunch, so see it before you sit down to eat, not after.
todo: Three Graces mosaic in the bath house
Grilled fish on a platform over the water
Drink from the spring by the quay
rev: The setting and the fish get consistent praise; the recurring complaints are that the museum is one small room for the price, parking is chaotic and the shoreline is rock, not sand.
entry: Mosaic museum ₺100 (≈€2.30) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 2 h west on the D400; it is signposted directly off the coast road below the Heaven and Hell turning.

name: Anemurium
desc: A Roman and early Byzantine city abandoned on the southernmost cape of Anatolia, its streets running downhill to a grey pebble beach. Three bath complexes still stand vaulted to roof height, and above them spreads a necropolis of some three hundred two-storey tomb houses, several with painted plaster and mosaic floors intact.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — July and August are merciless with zero shade
tip: Arrive two hours before sunset, walk the necropolis while the light is low, and swim off the site's own beach afterwards.
todo: Painted tombs in the necropolis
Vaulted baths and the odeon mosaic
Swim from the ruins' pebble beach
rev: Repeatedly described as the most underrated ruin on the coast and often visitor-free, though people warn about heat, snakes in the tomb rubble, the rough final track and very little interpretation.
onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) airport, then about 2 h 30 east on the D400; from Adana it is a long 5 h drive west.

name: Mamure Castle
desc: A castle standing directly on the beach with thirty-nine towers, a water-filled moat and palm trees growing in the courtyard. Roman in origin, rebuilt by the Karamanids and kept in use by the Ottomans into the nineteenth century, it is one of the few Turkish castles you enter across a proper drawbridge causeway.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the walls throw no shade at midday
tip: Walk the seaward rampart in the last hour before closing, when the storks are on the towers and the light comes off the water.
todo: Wall walk along the seaward rampart
Courtyard mosque and hamam ruins
The moat and its terrapins
rev: Visitors call it the most complete castle on the south coast and cheap for what it is, while grumbling about long restoration closures, missing handrails on the wall walk and the traffic noise from the D400.
onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) airport, then 2 h 15 east on the D400; the castle is 6 km east of Anamur town, on the seaward side of the road.

name: Tarsus
desc: Saint Paul's home town, layered rather than pretty. Cleopatra's Gate stands at the old harbour road, a stretch of Roman street lies four metres below today's pavement behind glass, and a well in a courtyard is shown as Paul's, complete with a bucket you can drink from. Restored Ottoman houses fill the block around it.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the Çukurova humidity in July and August is genuinely unpleasant
tip: Walk the excavated Roman road at the end of the day, then drive out to the waterfall for tea and fried fish where the town actually goes.
todo: Cleopatra's Gate and the old harbour road
Saint Paul's Well and the Roman street
Tea by the Tarsus waterfall
rev: Pilgrims and history readers rate the concentration of sites in ten walkable blocks; almost everyone mentions the sticky heat, the heavy traffic and how modest Cleopatra's Gate looks in the flesh.
entry: Mostly free; Saint Paul's Well and the museum around ₺100 (≈€2.30) each
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 30 min on the O-51; Adana–Mersin trains stop at Tarsus roughly hourly.

name: Cehennemdere Valley
desc: A steep gorge in the Taurus behind Erdemli, protected for its Cilician fir and cedar forest. A cold stream drops through a series of small falls between walls of grey limestone, and the temperature falls fifteen degrees in the half-hour drive up from the coastal highway.
season: May–Oct — the forest road is unreliable after heavy winter rain
tip: The strict reserve core needs forestry permission, so aim for the picnic ground and stream below it, which does not.
todo: Walk the stream between the falls
Cilician fir stands above the gorge
Trout lunch at a village restaurant
rev: Day-trippers from Mersin come for the cold water and the shade and rate it highly in July; complaints centre on the unpaved final kilometres, weekend picnic litter and the absence of any marked trail.
entry: Free — a small forestry picnic-ground fee in summer
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 1 h 30 to Erdemli on the D400 and about 40 min up the forest road; a car is essential.

name: Aydıncık (Kelenderis)
desc: A small town on the emptiest stretch of Turkey's south coast, built over ancient Kelenderis, whose harbour mosaic shows the same bay in the fifth century. The water off Sancak Burnu is clear enough to snorkel from the rocks, and the hotels are family pensions rather than resorts.
season: Jun–Oct for the water; May and Nov for walking the coast
tip: Drive 15 km east to the Gilindire cave, where 250 steps drop from the cliff to an underground lake at sea level with water you can touch.
todo: Gilindire (Aynalıgöl) cave and its lake
Harbour mosaic of ancient Kelenderis
Snorkel off the rocks at Sancak Burnu
rev: People come for a coast with no tour buses and cheap fish, and mostly get it, but note the long drive from anywhere, limited food choice out of season and pebble rather than sand beaches.
onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) airport, then 1 h 45 east on the D400, or 3 h west from Mersin; the coast road is slow and winding either way.

name: The Cilician Gates
desc: The pass that every army between Alexander and the Crusaders used to get from the Anatolian plateau down to the Cilician plain: a cleft in the Taurus where the road, the old caravan track and a Roman rock-cut inscription share one narrow gorge. The motorway now tunnels past it at speed.
season: Apr–Nov — snow and fog close the old road in midwinter
tip: Leave the O-21 at Gülek and take the old road through the village; the actual gorge and the ruined Byzantine castle above it are invisible from the motorway.
todo: The narrow gorge on the old Gülek road
Gülek castle on its crag
Roman roadworks cut into the rock
rev: History-minded drivers find the sense of the choke point still legible and the climb spectacular, but many arrive expecting a monument and find only rock, guardrails and lorries.
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 45 min north-west on the O-21 towards Niğde; take the Gülek exit for the old road.

name: Adana Stone Bridge
desc: A Roman bridge that has carried traffic over the Seyhan for nearly nineteen centuries and now carries only pedestrians. Fourteen of its original twenty-one arches survive, lit at night, linking the old bazaar quarter with the riverside parks where the whole city walks after dark in summer.
season: Year-round — evenings only from June to September, when daytime hits 40 °C
tip: Cross from the Ulu Cami side at dusk so the mosque, the bridge and the river come at you in the right order.
todo: Walk the bridge after dark
Ulu Cami and its black-and-white stonework
Riverside tea gardens on Merkez Park
rev: Locals and visitors alike treat the evening crossing as the best free thing in Adana; the usual complaints are heavy-handed restoration, the river's smell in late summer and persistent hawkers at both ends.
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 40 min into the city; the bridge is a 15-min walk from the old bazaar.

name: Sabancı Central Mosque
desc: A 1998 mosque of deliberately imperial ambition on the bank of the Seyhan: six minarets, a 54-metre dome and room for tens of thousands, built with Sabancı family money in a classical Ottoman idiom. Seen across the water at dusk with the Stone Bridge in front of it, the theatre works.
season: Year-round — visit in the early morning or after sunset in July and August
tip: Photograph it from the far bank near the Merkez Park footbridge rather than from the forecourt, where you cannot get the minarets in.
todo: Interior tilework under the main dome
Riverbank view with the Stone Bridge
Evening prayer call from six minarets
rev: Visitors are impressed by the sheer scale and the calm inside, while a good number find it a modern pastiche of Ottoman architecture and note that the tourist entrance and dress rules are enforced strictly.
entry: Free — modest dress, headscarves lent at the door
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 40 min into Adana; it stands beside the Stone Bridge on the west bank.

name: Varda Viaduct
desc: A German-built stone arch railway bridge of 1912 on the old Baghdad Railway, 98 metres above the Çakıt gorge near Karaisalı. Trains still cross it. Most people know it as the bridge Bond falls from in the opening of Skyfall, and the regional train from Adana stops at Hacıkırı right beside it.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the gorge is an oven in high summer
tip: Take the cheap Adana–Karaisalı regional train rather than driving: you cross the viaduct instead of just looking at it, and it costs less than a coffee.
todo: Ride the regional train across it
Viewpoint above Hacıkırı station
Old railway tunnels along the Çakıt
rev: The train ride is the part people rave about; the complaints are that walking out onto the bridge is now fenced off and policed, the timetable is sparse, and the viewpoint involves a dusty scramble.
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 1 h by road to Karaisalı, or take the local train from Adana station to Hacıkırı.

name: Anavarza (Anazarbus)
desc: A Roman city on the cotton plain with a triumphal arch still standing, a colonnaded street running for over two kilometres and mosaics under shelters, all beneath a knife-edge rock ridge carrying an Armenian castle. It was the capital of Cilician Armenia, and the castle walk along the ridge is the best thing in the province.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the plain routinely passes 40 °C in July and August
tip: Start the castle path from behind the village mosque with two litres of water; it is 45 hot minutes up and there is nothing at the top.
todo: Triumphal arch and colonnaded street
Ridge walk to the Armenian castle
Mosaics in the village museum
rev: People who make the climb call the ridge castle unforgettable and are astonished to be alone there; the standard warnings are heat, snakes, no shade, no water and a rough track for the last few kilometres.
entry: Small fee — check locally; the village mosaic museum is separate
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then about 1 h 15 north-east via Ceyhan and Kozan; there is no useful public transport.

name: Yılankale (Snake Castle)
desc: An Armenian castle of about 1200 clamped to a bare rock above the Ceyhan river, its curtain walls following every kink of the crag. Local stories make it the house of Şahmaran, the half-woman half-snake of Cilician folklore. Twenty-five minutes of scrambling puts you on walls with the whole Çukurova underneath.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the rock reflects heat viciously in summer
tip: Go in the last two hours of daylight and wear proper shoes; the path is loose limestone with no railings and no lighting on the way down.
todo: Scramble to the upper ward
Vaulted cistern inside the keep
Sunset over the Ceyhan plain
rev: Rated highly by anyone who likes empty castles with big views, and criticised for exactly what makes it good: no guardrails, no signs, no ticket office, no water and a scramble that is not for small children.
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 45 min east on the O-52 towards Ceyhan; the rock is visible from the motorway.

name: Yumurtalık
desc: Medieval Ayas, the port Marco Polo sailed from in 1271, now a low-key beach town where Adana empties itself at weekends. A ruined sea tower stands offshore, the fish restaurants are cheap, and the lagoons east of town are a protected reserve with flamingos, pelicans and nesting sea turtles.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; Nov–Mar for the birds on the lagoons
tip: Skip the town beach and drive to the Yumurtalık lagoon reserve at first light, when the flamingo flocks are still on the near shore.
todo: The offshore Genoese sea tower
Flamingos in the lagoon reserve
Fish and şalgam on the harbour front
rev: Weekenders like the prices, the fish and the fact that no one is selling anything; the honest downsides are the oil terminal and İskenderun industry on the skyline, murky water after storms and near-total gridlock on August Sundays.
entry: Free; lagoon reserve free but the tracks need a high car
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then about 1 h 15 east via Ceyhan; summer minibuses run from Adana otogar.

name: Kapıkaya Canyon
desc: A narrow limestone canyon on the Çakıt below Karaisalı, walked on a wooden boardwalk bolted to the rock a couple of metres above cold green water. It is short, maybe an hour there and back, and it pairs naturally with the Varda viaduct twenty minutes away.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — spring meltwater can close the boardwalk
tip: Come on a weekday; at weekends the boardwalk becomes a single-file queue of Adana families with picnic coolers.
todo: Boardwalk through the narrows
Swim in the cold pools at the end
Combine with the Varda viaduct
rev: Visitors call it a genuine relief from Çukurova heat and good for children, while complaining about weekend crowding, slippery planks, litter at the entrance and a car park attendant with informal pricing.
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 1 h north-west via Karaisalı; the last few kilometres are narrow but paved.

name: Adana Kebap and Şalgam
desc: Hand-minced lamb with tail fat pressed onto a wide flat skewer over oak charcoal, served with sumac onions, grilled long peppers and a glass of şalgam, the salty fermented juice of turnip and black carrot. The city eats liver kebab for breakfast at seven in the morning and treats the whole thing as a licensed ritual.
season: Year-round — Oct–May is more comfortable for eating outdoors
tip: Ask for acılı şalgam and order ciğer at breakfast rather than dinner; that is when the liver is fresh and when the kebapçıs around Kazancılar are full.
todo: Liver kebab breakfast near the old bazaar
Half-portion kebap with sumac onions
Bitter şalgam with chilli
rev: Nearly everyone says Adana kebap in Adana is a different dish from Adana kebap elsewhere; the caveats are the fat content, the fierce chilli in the local version and the heat and diesel of the bazaar in summer.
entry: Free — a portion with şalgam and bread around ₺400–600 (≈€9–13)
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 40 min into the centre; the kebap houses cluster around the old bazaar and Kuruköprü.

name: Karatepe-Aslantaş
desc: A late Hittite hill fort of the eighth century BC in pine woods above a reservoir, where the carved gate slabs are still set where they were found. The banquet scenes, ships and a mother nursing a child under a tree sit alongside the bilingual Phoenician and Luwian inscription that finally allowed hieroglyphic Luwian to be read.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the site closes early in winter and the woods are wet
tip: The reliefs are shown open-air in situ under shelters on a one-way woodland circuit, so allow an hour rather than the twenty minutes people plan.
todo: Bilingual inscription at the south gate
Banquet and ship reliefs in situ
Picnic under the pines above the lake
rev: Anyone with an interest in the Hittite world rates it among Turkey's most rewarding small sites; the complaints are the long approach road, restricted photography in places and a guardian who moves groups along briskly.
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then about 1 h 45 north-east via Kadirli; the last 20 km run through forest with no signage in English.

name: Hierapolis Castabala
desc: A colonnaded street of standing columns running straight across a cotton plain, with a medieval castle on the crag behind it. This was the sanctuary of Artemis Perasia, whose priestesses were said to walk barefoot over hot coals. Nothing is fenced, nobody sells tickets, and the columns are usually shared with grazing sheep.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the plain is 40 °C and shadeless in summer
tip: Go late in the afternoon when the low sun lines up the whole colonnade, and walk up to the castle for the view back down over it.
todo: Walk the length of the colonnade
Climb to the castle on the crag
Theatre seats among the thistles
rev: Visitors are surprised such a photogenic site is empty and free, and equally surprised by the total absence of facilities, shade, signage and any way of getting there without a car.
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then about 1 h 30 east on the O-52 and 10 km north of Osmaniye.

name: Zorkun Yayla
desc: Osmaniye's summer escape, 1,550 metres up in the pine and juniper of the Nur Mountains, reached by twenty-six kilometres of switchbacks off the hot plain. It is a working yayla of wooden summer houses, cold spring taps, tea gardens and afternoon mist that comes over the ridge like a lid.
season: Jun–Sep — snowbound and largely shuttered from December to March
tip: Come on a weekday and be up there before four, because the fog usually rolls in from the Mediterranean side by late afternoon and takes the view with it.
todo: Drink from the spring taps at Olukbaşı
Walk the forest tracks along the ridge
Gözleme in a yayla tea garden
rev: Turkish visitors love the twenty-degree temperature drop and the pine air; foreign visitors note the ramshackle building, weekend traffic on a narrow road and that there is little to do beyond walking and eating.
onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 1 h 30 east to Osmaniye and about 45 min of mountain road; dolmuşes run up in summer.

name: Antakya Old Town
desc: Ancient Antioch, and until February 2023 the finest surviving Arab-Turkish old town in the country: stone courtyard houses, a covered bazaar, and Habib-i Neccar, the oldest mosque in Anatolia. The earthquakes flattened most of it. What you visit now is a reconstruction site with pockets of restored street, and a food culture that refused to die.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — verify what is open before you commit to the trip
tip: Eat first and sightsee second: the künefe and the Antakya breakfast spreads came back long before the buildings did.
todo: Künefe made with fresh Antakya cheese
Habib-i Neccar mosque rebuilding site
Whatever of the Uzun Çarşı has reopened
rev: Recent visitors describe a city that is half building site and emotionally heavy going, while insisting the food and the hospitality are still the best in Türkiye; almost all advise checking hotel and restaurant status before travelling.
entry: Free to walk; individual monuments vary and several remain closed
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, back in service since late 2023, then 30 min into town; otherwise Çukurova (COV) and about 3 h by road.

name: Church of Saint Peter
desc: A cave hollowed into the flank of Mount Staurin above Antakya, claimed as one of the earliest Christian meeting places and traditionally linked to Peter himself. Behind the Crusader stone facade the interior is bare rock with a fragment of floor mosaic and a narrow escape tunnel cut into the hillside.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — check the reopening status before you plan around it
tip: The site was damaged in 2023 and access has come and gone since, so telephone the Hatay museum before driving up the hill.
todo: Rock-cut interior and floor mosaic
The escape tunnel behind the altar
View over Antakya from the terrace
rev: Pilgrims find the austerity moving and the setting on the mountainside striking; secular visitors often say it is one small cave for the ticket price, and everyone flags earthquake-related closures.
entry: €6 for foreigners when open · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye — verify before travelling
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 30 min to Antakya and 3 km up the hill road towards Reyhanlı; a taxi is easiest.

name: Hatay Archaeology Museum
desc: One of the largest collections of Roman mosaics anywhere, most of it lifted from the villas of Daphne just up the valley. The Buffet mosaic, Oceanus and Tethys, and the black-humoured Evil Eye panel are laid out at eye level in a purpose-built hall, so you read them as pictures rather than as floors.
season: Year-round — an obvious refuge on a 40 °C afternoon
tip: Start at the far end with the Yakto mosaic's border of everyday Antioch street scenes; it is the single most informative object in the building and most people walk past it.
todo: Yakto mosaic and its street-life border
Oceanus and Tethys panel
The Evil Eye mosaic
rev: Mosaic enthusiasts routinely call it world-class and better presented than Zeugma; complaints are thin English labelling, gallery closures for post-earthquake works, and the fact that the city outside gives you nothing else to do.
entry: €9 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 30 min into Antakya; the museum is on the ring road at the edge of the centre.

name: Vakıflı
desc: The last Armenian village in Türkiye, about a hundred people on the seaward slope of Musa Dağı among orange and laurel groves. There is one church, Surp Asdvadzadzin, a co-operative selling laurel soap and bitter orange jam, and a dialect of Western Armenian that other Armenians struggle to follow.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the citrus harvest runs through late autumn
tip: Buy from the village co-operative rather than the roadside stalls below; the laurel soap and the jam are made a hundred metres from where they are sold.
todo: Surp Asdvadzadzin church
Laurel soap and orange jam from the co-op
View down to the Orontes mouth
rev: Visitors describe an ordinary, slightly weary farming village rather than a museum, which is the point; some feel intrusive, and post-earthquake damage and a very small ageing population are visible.
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then about 1 h via Samandağ and a short climb up the Musa Dağı road.

name: Samandağ
desc: Fourteen kilometres of dark volcanic sand where the Orontes finally reaches the sea, backed by an Arab-Alawite farming district with its own food, dialect and calendar. Green and loggerhead turtles nest along the beach, and the small port of Çevlik at the northern end sits on ancient Seleucia Pieria.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — turtle nesting restricts parts of the beach in high summer
tip: Eat where the signs are in Arabic as well as Turkish, and ask for oruk and the local hummus, which is nothing like the Istanbul version.
todo: Walk the dark-sand beach at dusk
Çevlik harbour and its Roman quays
Alawite home cooking in a village lokanta
rev: People value the emptiness, the food and the lack of resorts, but are blunt about plastic and driftwood along the tideline, the earthquake rubble dumped near the coast after 2023 and the shortage of decent accommodation.
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then about 1 h west over the hills from Antakya; minibuses run from Antakya to Samandağ all day.

name: Titus Tunnel
desc: A flood-diversion channel nearly 1,400 metres long, cut through solid rock by legionaries and prisoners to stop a mountain torrent silting up the harbour of Seleucia Pieria. You walk through it: open-air trench with walls thirty metres high, then a long roofed section where the chisel marks are still crisp on the rock.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — after heavy rain water runs through the tunnel floor
tip: Climb the path above the tunnel mouth to the Beşikli cave tombs, rock-cut family graves most people miss entirely.
todo: Walk the roofed section end to end
Roman chisel marks and the dedication
Beşikli rock-cut tombs above
rev: Engineering-minded visitors find it astonishing for the price and love that you can actually walk it; the usual gripes are slippery wet rock, no lighting, uneven steps and thin signposting from the coast road.
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 1 h to Samandağ and 4 km on to Çevlik; the last stretch is signposted from the harbour.

name: Musa Dağı
desc: A 1,280-metre limestone ridge dropping straight into the sea, wooded with pine and carob and cut by shepherd tracks. In 1915 the people of six Armenian villages held out on this mountain for forty days until French warships took them off, the episode Franz Werfel turned into a novel. The view runs from the Orontes delta to Syria.
season: Apr–Jun and Oct–Nov — summer is too hot for the ascent and winter fog sits on the ridge
tip: There is no waymarked route to the top, so start from Vakıflı and ask in the village; going up blind on forest tracks wastes a day.
todo: Ridge walk above the citrus terraces
Viewpoint over the Orontes delta
Read the Werfel story before you go
rev: Walkers rate the sea views and the emptiness; the honest picture is unmarked paths, no water on the ridge, ticks in spring, sensitivity about the border zone and nothing at all in the way of infrastructure.
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 1 h to Samandağ; drive up through Vakıflı and park where the asphalt ends.

name: Harbiye (Daphne)
desc: The laurel-shaded ravine eight kilometres south of Antakya that Roman Antioch used as its pleasure suburb. Springs drop through a series of small falls between plane trees, and the mosaics that made the Hatay museum famous were lifted from villas on these slopes. Tea platforms are built out over the water.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the water is thinnest in late summer
tip: Walk to the upper falls above the café terraces, where the noise drops away and the laurel smell is strongest.
todo: Upper falls above the tea gardens
Buy defne laurel soap at source
Lunch on a platform over the stream
rev: The cool and the noise of water are the draw, especially in July; visitors complain that cafés have colonised almost every viewpoint, that litter builds up at weekends and that the falls are smaller than the photographs suggest.
entry: Free to enter the valley; café terraces expect an order
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 30 min; Antakya–Harbiye dolmuşes leave every few minutes from the city.

name: Yayladağı and Kel Dağı
desc: Türkiye's southernmost district, a cool forested upland pressed against the Syrian border. Above it rises Kel Dağı, ancient Mount Casius, holy to Baal Zaphon and later to Zeus, at 1,726 metres the highest thing on this coast. The town below was badly damaged in 2023 and is still rebuilding.
season: May–Oct — winter brings fog, snow and closed forest roads
tip: The summit sits in a military zone and needs permission, so plan for the forest roads and viewpoints below it rather than the top.
todo: Forest roads under Kel Dağı
Viewpoint over the Syrian plain
Village breakfast with mountain honey
rev: Those who go describe genuinely wild country and total absence of tourism; they also report checkpoints, patchy phone signal, earthquake damage in the town and confusion over where you are and are not allowed to walk.
entry: Free — carry your passport for the checkpoints
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then about 1 h 15 south of Antakya on a good but winding road.

name: Belen Pass
desc: The Syrian Gates of antiquity: the road climbs from the Gulf of İskenderun to 750 metres through pine forest and a permanent cold wind, with the whole bay laid out behind you. Cyrus, Alexander and every caravan to Aleppo came this way. At the western foot stands the Pillar of Jonah, where the prophet was supposedly put ashore.
season: Year-round — fog and ice are common on the top in January and February
tip: Take the old road over the pass instead of the motorway tunnel and stop at a roadside grill in Belen town for the local mountain cheese.
todo: Viewpoint over the Gulf of İskenderun
Roadside grill in Belen village
Pillar of Jonah at the western foot
rev: Drivers enjoy the temperature drop and the view back over the bay, while noting heavy lorry traffic on the old road, a scruffy strip of development in Belen itself and little to mark the historic pass.
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 45 min north; the pass sits on the old road between İskenderun and Antakya.

name: Arsuz
desc: Ancient Rhosus, and the one stretch of Hatay coast people actually swim from: a long shallow bay of coarse sand under the Amanus, a seafront promenade of İskenderun families, and fish restaurants that serve Arab mezze alongside the standard raki table. Quiet and cheap outside July and August.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct for the promenade without crowds
tip: Sit down to eat where the mezze arrive unasked on a tray to choose from; that is the Hatay convention and it is how you find the good tables.
todo: Evening walk along the seafront
Arab mezze with grilled fish
Swim from the southern end of the bay
rev: Regulars praise the value and the food and say the sea is cleaner than İskenderun's; the standard complaints are the industrial skyline to the north, unremarkable modern building and a very Turkish rather than international resort feel.
onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then about 1 h via İskenderun and the coast road south.

name: Kahramanmaraş Castle
desc: A castle mound in the middle of the city, occupied since Hittite times and rebuilt by Romans, Armenians, Dulkadirs and Ottomans in turn. The famous Maraş lion came off this hill. Since February 2023 it has stood over a city rebuilding itself, and parts of the walls are under restoration scaffolding.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the summer plain is brutally hot, winter cold and grey
tip: Check with the city museum whether the ramp to the upper walls has reopened before climbing the hill, and combine it with the archaeological museum below.
todo: View over the rebuilding city
Hittite lion in the museum
Coffee in the restored quarter below
rev: Visitors value the view and the layered history, but are honest that access has been intermittent since the earthquakes, restoration works block parts of the circuit and the surrounding streets are a construction site.
entry: Free when open; the museum around ₺150 (≈€3.50) · Museum Pass Türkiye accepted
onward: Kahramanmaraş (KCM) airport, then 30 min into town; Çukurova (COV) is about 2 h 30 by road.

name: Yedikuyular Ski Centre
desc: A small ski area on Ahır Dağı at around 2,000 to 2,300 metres, twenty-five kilometres above Kahramanmaraş. Two lifts, a handful of pistes and a plateau that looks straight down onto the Çukurova haze. It is a locals' hill: cheap lift passes, families on hired gear, and Maraş ice cream at the base station in the snow.
season: Late Dec–Mar for snow; Jun–Sep for the plateau meadows and paragliding
tip: Go midweek and hire everything at the base; weekend queues at the single chairlift eat most of the skiing day.
todo: Day on the chairlift pistes
Snow picnic with Maraş dondurma
Summer walk on the Ahır Dağı plateau
rev: Turkish skiers rate it as excellent value with reliable January snow; the caveats are very few runs, one chairlift, patchy snowmaking and a short access road that ices up.
onward: Kahramanmaraş (KCM) airport, then 30 min to the city and about 45 min up the mountain road.

name: Döngel Caves
desc: A cave system in the hills north of Kahramanmaraş where a stream still runs through the lower galleries and travertine curtains hang in chambers big enough to lose a group in. Above the village a waterfall drops into a pool with trout restaurants on the bank, which is why most people actually come.
season: May–Oct — the access road is unreliable when snow lies on the hills
tip: Bring your own torch; the fixed lighting works only in the developed section and the interesting galleries start where it stops.
todo: Travertine chambers in the show section
Döngel waterfall and its pool
Trout lunch at the village
rev: Domestic visitors like the combination of cave, waterfall and cheap trout; they warn about the rough last stretch of road, mud underfoot in the cave, weak lighting and weekend crowds at the restaurants.
onward: Kahramanmaraş (KCM) airport, then about 1 h 15 north of the city on progressively narrower roads; a car is essential.

name: Maraş Ice Cream
desc: Goat milk, sugar and salep root from the mountains above the city, beaten in a churn until it is elastic enough to cut with a knife and eat with a fork. In its home town it is served in slabs on a plate, not in cones, and the theatrical vendor act that tourists know from Istanbul is largely absent.
season: Year-round — the old shops keep going through winter, which is when locals prefer it
tip: Order it kesme, cut in slices on a plate with a knife and fork, and eat it in one of the long-established shops in the centre rather than a chain kiosk.
todo: Kesme dondurma on a plate
Watch the churn being worked
Buy salep to take home
rev: Almost everyone says the texture is a different product from supermarket ice cream and worth the detour; the criticisms are how sweet and chewy it is, inflated prices in tourist-facing shops and short opening hours.
entry: Free — a plate of kesme dondurma around ₺150 (≈€3.50)
onward: Kahramanmaraş (KCM) airport, then 30 min into the centre; the historic shops are within walking distance of each other.

name: Germanicia Mosaics
desc: A Roman city found by accident in 2007 when looters dug through a garden in a residential quarter of Kahramanmaraş. Under metal shelters between apartment blocks lie fifth and sixth-century villa floors with hunting scenes, animals and geometric borders in remarkably fresh colour. Excavation continues in gaps between houses.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the shelters get very hot in midsummer
tip: Ask at the city archaeological museum first; the shelters are locked and a guardian has to come and open them for you.
todo: Hunting-scene villa floor
Compare with the museum's finds
See the excavation between apartment blocks
rev: Those who get inside call the mosaics unexpectedly fine for a site nobody has heard of; the recurring frustration is erratic opening, no signage, no English information and post-earthquake disruption to the district.
entry: Small fee — check locally at the Kahramanmaraş museum
onward: Kahramanmaraş (KCM) airport, then 30 min into the city; the site is inside the Dulkadiroğlu quarter, easiest by taxi.

name: Lake Eğirdir and Yeşilada
desc: Türkiye's second-largest freshwater lake, held between bare limestone ridges and turning genuinely turquoise in the shallows. The town sits on a promontory under a Seljuk castle, and a causeway runs out to Yeşilada, an old Greek fishing island of stone houses now full of small pensions and a ruined church.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — swimming is realistic from late June to September
tip: Sleep on Yeşilada, not in the town: the pensions on the island face west and the sunset from their terraces is the reason to come.
todo: Sunset from a Yeşilada terrace
Fried lake fish and apple orchards
Start of the St Paul Trail above town
rev: Walkers and cyclists rate it as the best-value lake base in Türkiye; the honest complaints are the falling water level, algae blooms in hot summers, concrete on the causeway and a military zone occupying part of the promontory.
onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then 45 min, or Antalya (AYT) and about 2 h 30 over the Taurus; buses run from Isparta every hour.

name: Lake Kovada National Park
desc: A small forested lake south of Eğirdir, fed by the canal that drains it, ringed by pine and oak with trails along the shore. It is one of the quietest national parks in the country: no boats, no cafés, a barrier, a fee, and an hour or two of walking with wild boar tracks in the mud.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — mosquitoes in July, and the lake shrinks badly in drought years
tip: Combine it with the drive on to Yazılı canyon; on its own Kovada is a half-day at most and there is nowhere to eat inside the park.
todo: Shore trail through the pine woods
Look for otter and boar tracks
Picnic at the northern inlet
rev: Visitors describe real quiet and clean air and are glad they came; they also report minimal facilities, unmarked side trails, low water in late summer and a fee that feels steep for what is provided.
entry: ₺150 (≈€3.50) per person plus a vehicle fee
onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 1 h 15 via Eğirdir; there is no public transport to the gate.

name: Yazılı Canyon
desc: A cold green gorge in the Taurus above Sütçüler, with plane trees, pools you can swim in and a Greek inscription on the rock that gives the canyon its name. The Roman Via Sebaste ran through here, and the modern St Paul Trail follows the same line along the water.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct for walking without the crowds
tip: Walk beyond the first bridge where the day-trippers stop; the good pools and the inscription are another twenty minutes upstream.
todo: Swim in the cold upstream pools
Find the rock inscription
Trout at the park restaurant
rev: Walkers rate the water and the shade highly in July; the complaints are the winding 80 km approach from Isparta, crowded weekends, litter near the entrance and water cold enough to hurt.
entry: ₺150 (≈€3.50) per person plus a small vehicle fee
onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 1 h 45 south via Sütçüler, or 2 h north from Antalya (AYT).

name: Antiochia in Pisidia
desc: A Roman colony on a terrace above Yalvaç where Paul preached the first sermon recorded in Acts. The sanctuary of Augustus sits on a rock platform cut into the hillside, the aqueduct arches still march across the slope, and the basilica of St Paul keeps a mosaic floor naming its donors.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — 1,200 m up, so cold and often snowy from December
tip: See the Yalvaç museum in town first; the fragments of the Latin Res Gestae inscription from the site are there, not on the hill.
todo: Augustus sanctuary platform
Mosaic floor in the St Paul basilica
Aqueduct arches on the hillside
rev: Biblical-route travellers find it rewarding and nearly empty; others say the ruins are low and hard to read without a guide, the wind on the terrace is fierce, and the site is a long way from anything else.
onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 1 h 45 round the north end of Lake Eğirdir to Yalvaç.

name: Isparta Rose Harvest
desc: For about four weeks from late May the plateau around Isparta smells of damask roses. Pickers are in the fields before dawn because the oil evaporates once the sun is up, and sacks of pink petals go straight to the distilleries at Gülbirlik and Gönen, where a tonne of petals yields a few hundred grams of oil.
season: Late May to mid-June only — outside that window there is nothing to see
tip: Be standing in a field between five and seven in the morning; by nine the picking is finished and the roses are gone for the day.
todo: Dawn picking in a village field
Distillery visit in Gönen or Keçiborlu
Rose jam and lokum at the co-op shop
rev: Those who time it right describe the smell as the whole point and worth the early alarm; the frequent disappointment is arriving in July to bare bushes, plus pushy roadside shops selling diluted rose oil.
entry: Free in the fields; distillery tours a small fee
onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then 20 min, or Antalya (AYT) and 2 h over the Taurus; the rose villages ring the city.

name: Mount Davraz
desc: A 2,635-metre Taurus peak with a ski centre on its northern flank, twenty-five kilometres from both Isparta and Eğirdir. From the top of the chairlift you can see Lake Eğirdir on one side and Burdur's salt lake on the other, and in summer the same lifts serve walkers on the summit ridge.
season: Jan–Mar for skiing; Jun–Sep for the ridge walk and the lake views
tip: Stay in Eğirdir rather than at the mountain hotels and drive up for the day; the lake town is cheaper, warmer and far better for eating.
todo: Chairlift to the two-lake viewpoint
Ski the long blue down the north face
Summer walk on the summit ridge
rev: Skiers call it quiet, cheap and surprisingly scenic; the drawbacks reported are inconsistent snow in warm winters, limited lift capacity at weekends and a resort base that is little more than a car park and two hotels.
entry: Day pass around ₺600 (≈€13) with hire extra
onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then 40 min to the base; Antalya (AYT) is about 2 h 30 by road over the pass.

name: Sagalassos
desc: A Pisidian mountain city at 1,500 metres on the flank of Akdağ, abandoned after earthquakes and never built over. The Antonine nymphaeum has been re-erected and mountain water pours through it again, the theatre leans into the slope with its seats intact, and the whole site looks out over an empty valley.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — snow can close the road from December to March
tip: Go in the morning before the cloud builds on Akdağ, and take a jacket; it is ten degrees colder up here than in Burdur.
todo: Water running in the Antonine fountain
Theatre seats above the valley
Upper agora and the Hadrian find spot
rev: Repeatedly described as the most spectacularly sited ruin in Türkiye and better excavated than most; complaints are the steep walking on loose ground, the exposed cold wind and the 7 km of hairpins up from Ağlasun.
onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 1 h via Ağlasun, or 2 h 30 from Antalya (AYT); a car is effectively required.

name: Ağlasun
desc: The small town seven kilometres below Sagalassos, and the reason to stay the night rather than day-trip. Old stone and timber houses run up the valley, plane trees shade the square, water runs in channels along the streets, and the pensions fill each summer with the Belgian archaeologists who dig the site above.
season: May–Oct — quiet and cold once the excavation season ends
tip: Eat at the square in the evening and ask about a lift up to the ruins for opening time; the pensions arrange it far cheaper than a taxi from Burdur.
todo: Evening in the plane-tree square
Ottoman houses on the upper lanes
Friday village market
rev: Travellers value the price, the quiet and the walking access to Sagalassos; they also point out there is almost nothing to do after dark, few rooms, and no alcohol served in most places.
onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 50 min south-west; buses run from Burdur and Isparta a few times a day.

name: Lake Salda
desc: A deep crater lake ringed in places by brilliant white hydromagnesite sand, which turns the shallows the colour of a tropical lagoon. NASA studied it as an analogue for Jezero crater on Mars. The water is alkaline, very clear and cold, and the white shore is now fenced and protected after years of being trampled.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct for the colours without the buses
tip: The famous white beach is a protected zone reached by shuttle with no swimming in parts, so go to the eastern public beach if you actually want to get in the water.
todo: White shore at the protected zone
Swim from the eastern public beach
Walk the pine slope above the water
rev: Everyone agrees the colour is real and remarkable; the standard complaints are Instagram crowds, restrictions and shuttles introduced to save the shoreline, mud-smearing visitors, and a lake level that keeps dropping.
entry: Public beach around ₺100 (≈€2.30) plus parking; the protected zone runs a shuttle
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) airport, then about 1 h 15, or Isparta (ISE) and 1 h 45; Antalya is 3 h over the mountains.

name: İnsuyu Cave
desc: Turkey's first show cave, opened in 1965: about six hundred metres of walkway past stalactite galleries to a chain of underground lakes, of which the Great Lake is the one people come for. Groundwater extraction in the valley above has dried the lakes out in bad years, and the cave has closed and reopened repeatedly because of it.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — a constant 14 °C inside whatever the season
tip: Ring ahead and ask whether the lakes actually have water in them; without them it is a short walk past dry formations.
todo: Walkway to the Great Lake
Stalactite galleries near the entrance
Cool off on a 40 °C afternoon
rev: When the lakes are full people call it a genuine surprise; reviews from dry years are flat, and there are regular grumbles about slippery steps, weak lighting and long closures for maintenance.
onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 1 h; the cave is 13 km south of Burdur on the Antalya road.

name: Kibyra
desc: A city of horse breeders and ironworkers on a ridge above Gölhisar, with a stadium that still seats ten thousand almost intact. The real object is in the odeon: a floor of coloured marble laid as a Medusa head more than five metres across, one of the few of its kind anywhere.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — 1,000 m up, so cold and wet in winter
tip: The Medusa floor is covered over for protection outside the warm months, so confirm it is uncovered before making the drive.
todo: Medusa mosaic in the odeon
Walk the length of the stadium
Theatre and the ridge-top view
rev: Visitors find the stadium and the mosaic well worth a long detour and usually have the place to themselves; the complaints are the distance from everywhere, no shade, and the mosaic being under its winter cover.
onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) airport, then about 1 h 30 via Gölhisar; from Fethiye it is a 1 h 30 climb inland.

name: Lake Burdur
desc: A closed salt lake that winters most of the world's white-headed ducks, along with flamingos and thousands of waders. It is also a case study in disappearance: the shoreline has retreated kilometres since the 1970s as irrigation took the inflow, leaving pale salt flats and stranded jetties behind the birds.
season: Nov–Mar for the wintering ducks; Apr–May for waders on passage
tip: Bring binoculars and go to the northern shore near Karakent early; from the Burdur town side the birds are usually far out on the flats.
todo: White-headed ducks in winter
Salt flats where the water used to be
Burdur Museum's Sagalassos finds
rev: Birdwatchers rate the winter duck counts as internationally significant; everyone else notes there is no hide, no visitor centre, a lot of dust, and a shoreline that is bleak rather than beautiful.
onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then 50 min to Burdur; the north shore tracks need a car and dry weather.
